title: People
overview: Projects deliver change, and change lands on people. The chapter covers three people-focused activities that run through the whole method: leading successful change, leading successful teams, and communication. Expect questions on stakeholders, culture, the two approaches (change management, communication management) and how people factors show up in each principle.

sections.heading: Context
sections.keyMessage: A project delivers change that affects people in their business-as-usual work. How well it performs depends on the team's capability, the strength of their relationships and the people the change affects.
points: In PRINCE2, people means those working on the project, the relationships between them, and those impacted by it.

Organizations are complex ecosystems of changing relationships. Projects change organizations whether or not that is their main purpose, so a project must build strong relationships with the organizations that support delivery and fit into the wider ecosystem.
A project brings together people from the business, user and supplier communities for a limited time. Leaders at every level must build a project culture that motivates them.

Decisions belong close to where the relevant knowledge sits. Escalate only when the impact on other parts of the project or organizational ecosystem, or wider political implications, must be considered.

Organizational ecosystem: the internal elements of an organization (staff, board, owners, other stakeholders) plus its external relationships (customers, partners, suppliers, regulators, competitors). Project ecosystem: the elements of the business involved in or directly impacted by the project, plus its users and suppliers (Figure 3.1).

Scenario (Findef): four governance layers keep decisions at the right level. Stage gates, scope changes and supplier selection sit with the project board; programme and project tolerances and tranche sign-off with the programme board; investment changes over 20 per cent of the original programme budget with the investment committee; strategic decisions with the leadership board.

sections.heading: Projects require change management
points: Every project moves how people, organizations and systems operate from a current state to a target state that uses the project products. Effective leadership is needed to deliver that change.

Change management is the means by which an organization transitions from the current state to the target state. States can be described as routines, responsibilities, relationships, cultures and capabilities. There may be interim states too.

PRINCE2 handles this by creating and maintaining a change management approach. How much detail it holds depends on the decisions it supports, the skills needed during and after transition, the parts of the ecosystem affected, key relationships, evolving culture and how best to transition (learning, upskilling, transferring knowledge or recruiting).

The change management approach is part of the project initiation documentation. Its purpose is to establish the target organizational state needed for the project's objectives and the means of moving from the current state, through any interim states.

Its content: scope (changes delivered, exclusions); change states (current, interim, target); state characteristics (routines, practices, process, culture, responsibilities, structure, capabilities); enabling activities before, during and after transition (consultation, trials, training, helpline); resources; responsibilities; supporting tools and techniques; standards; references.

sections.heading: Stakeholders
points: A stakeholder is any individual, group or organization that can affect, or be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by, the project. They cover users, suppliers and the business, and can sit outside both the team and the business.
Understanding the relationships between the project and the organizational ecosystem, and identifying key stakeholders at the interface between the two, is fundamental to leading successful change.

Key influencers include senior executives; people in the user, supplier and operational communities who do day-to-day work and make decisions; people found at bottlenecks where information, knowledge and money cross interfaces (document controllers, technical experts, commercial managers); people who shape the majority's perception; and the people the team must work with most closely.

Influencers have the greatest effect on adoption of the project products and on realizing the benefits. Understanding their perspectives and constraints improves delivery. The stakeholders at the interface can change as the project evolves.
Set the project up to support relationship building across interfaces, for example regular meetings and working groups that build shared understanding of perspectives, data and knowledge.

Figure 3.2: the business, user and supplier interests each sit partly in the organizational ecosystem and partly in the project ecosystem, and the proportions differ by project. Knowing where each interest sits helps decide how it is represented and engaged.

sections.heading: Culture
points: Culture is the set of shared attitudes, values, goals and ways of working that characterize a group of people.
Teams combine people from different working cultures. A project may need its own culture, distinct from the business but aligned with the wider ecosystem.

A shared understanding of the project, developed with key influencers, is captured in the project brief. Combined with legal and regulatory obligations and business commitments (such as sustainability targets) it guides decisions at several layers.

From that shared understanding the team sets ways of working, captured in the management approaches. Who is assigned to project roles, including board members who represent business, user and supplier interests, also builds it.
The team structure and the quality and planning practices make sure users are represented or involved in defining, developing and quality-checking products, and consulted in decisions.
At the start the project culture mirrors the organization's; a distinct one may emerge. Formal ways of working should evolve with it.
Check the shared understanding at the end of each stage and whenever key influencers change.

Persistent non-compliance with project processes is often a leading indicator that the agreed ways of working no longer fit the emerging culture. Do not assume poor behaviour; explore the underlying disconnect.

Scenario (NowByou): the contracted project manager formed a community of practice, the project club, to co-create the toolkit from existing artefacts (the campaign brief became the project brief), with roadshows planned to embed it.

sections.heading: Leading successful teams
points: Collaboration: people across the project ecosystem working together toward the objectives. Co-creation: a form of collaboration involving users and key influencers in designing products and ways of working so they are adopted. Leadership: motivating people toward the objectives, by collaborating, persuading, influencing and co-creating, managing key relationships and seeking regular feedback. Management: instructing the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working; co-creating those ways of working makes people more willing to be managed by them.
Project teams are temporary and cross organizational boundaries, so people often have several reporting lines (to the allocating organization, a supplier, or multiple projects when part-time).

Things to be aware of: the project manager's formal authority sits within the board's tolerances but the real power structure may differ; project managers rely on influence, motivation and aligned interests; PRINCE2 roles may not match job titles; team members have competing priorities; some members may be more senior than the project manager; some motivators (pay, career progression) are outside the project manager's remit.
These factors mean project teams need a different style of management and leadership from established business teams, because a temporary leader finds it harder to exercise authority.

sections.heading: Leading across organizational boundaries
points: Some people are affected by the project but are not in the project team. They may contribute directly (defining, assuring, accepting products) or indirectly (upskilling staff, changing ways of working, integrating products into their area).
If that work falls outside project scope, make clear the dependencies, who is responsible, and how it is funded and monitored. Otherwise projects can be delayed or miss their benefits.
Leading beyond direct authority needs cultural intelligence: the capability to relate and work across cultures within the organizational ecosystem.

Working across cultures needs: teams that adapt and find ways to interface; clear project boundaries within which people can flex; the right conditions for people to succeed; awareness of different perspectives (often called emotional intelligence); and awareness of the constraints on people's time and attention.

sections.heading: Building effective teams
points: An effective team has a diverse mix of capabilities, competencies and perspectives that match the project. Organizations cannot always pick ideal people, so identify gaps and mitigate them (upskilling, moving tasks to better-suited people).
People with the same competencies still perform a role differently, and the same person may perform differently with different colleagues.
Temporary teams may not have worked together, so structured exercises that build self-awareness, self-management and understanding of others help to build trust and compatible ways of working.
Roles and responsibilities should reflect each person's capability, authority and availability, viewed through their key relationships, and be reviewed when those relationships shift.

Psychological safety: members feel accepted, respected and able to voice diverse views without fear of negative consequences. All members are responsible for creating it and for each other's wellbeing. Teams may also need room to experiment, inspect, adapt and self-organize.

PRINCE2 supports effective teams through: the project plan (clear purpose, answers stakeholder questions); the team structure and role descriptions (roles, relationships, coaching or training needs); the communication management approach (how members engage and relationships develop); the project initiation documentation (agreed ways of working); and product-based planning (agreed product descriptions, dependencies and sequencing).

sections.heading: Bringing the team together
points: However the team works (virtual, in person, hybrid), consider how to use people's time well and build social cohesion.

Social cohesion is built by meeting purposefully and regularly to build trust across silos; planning how key relationships will be developed and kept over the project so there is resilience when hurdles arise; and considering co-location, which allows informal relationship building.

Virtual, remote or hybrid teams may need extra effort: synchronized co-location days for key people, time for unstructured online conversation, away days, virtual collaboration tools, and chances or incentives to meet face to face.

Scenario (FindefTwo): after a hard stage across time zones, the project manager held a pause-and-reflect day to share lessons and build cohesion, and agreed regular update webinars at different times plus a virtual coffee time.

sections.heading: Communication
points: Projects create change and attract scrutiny and misconception. Without a clear approach to communication, barriers arise as people protect the current situation or limit its perceived harm.

PRINCE2 addresses communication in the communication management approach, part of the project initiation documentation. Its purpose is to define the means and frequency of communicating with, and getting feedback from, the project ecosystem, through a controlled, two-way flow of information.

Its content: scope; stakeholder analysis; communications schedule and procedures (per stakeholder group: purpose, frequency, channels, messaging); responsibilities; resources; supporting tools and techniques; standards (for example public engagement and ethical standards); references.

It is as much about listening as broadcasting: understand perceptions and concerns so they are addressed before they become risks, and tailor messages to each group. Generic messaging is rarely effective.

Work with key influencers from the user, supplier and business groups to get strong feedback loops and tailored messages. Messaging is hard to control in a connected digital landscape, so have influencers help shape it.
Most communication happens outside formal channels. Provide information in formats that are easy to share and give several routes for feedback.

Co-located teams: information moves organically, so offer shareable formats, monitor whether it flows freely and reconnect anyone disconnected. Remote teams: need a more deliberate, structured approach, with time for unstructured listening and sharing. Hybrid teams: make sure separate more-involved and less-involved groups do not form by location.

The approach evolves as the project becomes better defined. For complex, wide-impact or politically sensitive projects, a quiet phase keeps wider communication minimal while a small group of key influencers develops the project, limiting rumour and misinformation.

Periodic reporting alone is not enough because people may subconsciously bias what they report. Open, transparent environments reduce bias, but also build relationships with key influencers and monitor the health of key relationships.
Pockets of resistance show where communication should be focused: listen to the concerns to find misconceptions and address issues.

sections.heading: People are central to the method
points: Three people-focused activities: leading successful change, leading successful teams and communication. They are not standalone; they influence every aspect of project management and sit at the centre of the method (Figure 3.3).
PRINCE2 has five integrated elements: principles, people, practices, processes and the project context. The following sections show how the principles, practices and processes address people factors.

sections.heading: People and the principles
points: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships is the principle that keeps people factors addressed throughout the lifecycle.

Continued business justification: it must satisfy the user, business and supplier interests, which takes time; what counts as justification can change when roles change; it can be perception-based, so the communication management approach helps maintain it by managing relationships and showing progress.

Learn from experience: valuable knowledge is hidden in the ecosystem, so create a collaborative environment that shares it. Behaviours, culture and relationships are hard to document and are best learned socially, for example by talking to people from earlier stages or similar projects.

Manage by stages: stages often mark a change in influencers and key relationships and in organizational design. Stage boundaries are good points to review skills for the next stage and change people, even on the project board.

Manage by exception: decisions sit at the most local level that has the knowledge, and move up when they affect other areas or have wider impact. The extent of delegation depends on trust and confidence in the key relationships and adapts as skills develop.
Focus on products: co-creating products with agreed product descriptions across business, user and supplier unites perspectives, improves adoption and reduces handover risk.
Tailor: adapt the method to the people and organizations, not the reverse. Tailoring depends on capability or project management maturity, which grows over time.

Scenario (NowByou): the contracted project manager manages by exception with the skilled fast-learning future project manager, but uses closer direction, coaching and gradually more autonomy with the campaign team manager who lacks planning skills.

sections.heading: People and the practices
points: The seven practices are essential aspects of project management applied continually and in parallel throughout the project.

The organizing practice explains how people organize in a temporary project management team, ensures user, supplier and business interests are represented, and establishes the design and development of the organization.

People factors appear in all practices. For example, the business case needs perspectives from across the organizational ecosystem (business, user, supplier) to give clarity of purpose and a common understanding.

sections.heading: People and the processes
points: The processes are organized into four layers: business, directing, managing and delivering.
People factors such as behaviours, culture and relationships are included in the processes, showing how people interface between the layers (see Chapter 12).

terms.definition: The internal elements of an organization (staff, board, owners, other stakeholders) together with its external relationships such as customers, partners, suppliers, regulators and competitors.
Those elements of the business involved in or directly impacted by the project, and the associated users and suppliers.
The means by which an organization transitions from the current state to the target state.
Any individual, group or organization that can affect or be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by, the project.
The set of shared attitudes, values, goals and ways of working that characterize a group of people.
People from across the project ecosystem working together to achieve the project's objectives.
A specific form of collaboration involving users and key influencers in the design of products and agreed ways of working so they are adopted by the project and organizational ecosystems.
Motivating people to achieve a project's objectives, best done through collaboration, persuading, influencing and co-creating, managing key relationships and seeking regular feedback.
Instructing the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working.

cards.front: What does people cover in PRINCE2?
cards.back: Those working on the project, the relationships between them, and those impacted by the project.

cards.front: Organizational ecosystem versus project ecosystem?
cards.back: Organizational: an organization's internal elements plus its external relationships. Project: the parts of the business involved in or directly impacted by the project, plus its users and suppliers.

cards.front: When should a decision be escalated?
cards.back: Only when it affects other parts of the project or organizational ecosystem, or has wider political implications. Otherwise decide close to the relevant knowledge.

cards.front: Define change management.
cards.back: The means by which an organization transitions from the current state to the target state.

cards.front: What is the change management approach, and where does it sit?
cards.back: A management product, part of the project initiation documentation, establishing the target organizational state and how the business moves there through any interim states.

cards.front: Contents of the change management approach?
cards.back: Scope; change states; state characteristics; enabling activities; resources; responsibilities; supporting tools and techniques; standards; references.

cards.front: Define stakeholder.
cards.back: Any individual, group or organization that can affect or be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by, the project.

cards.front: Why do key influencers matter?
cards.back: They have the greatest influence on adoption of the project products and realization of benefits; working with them improves delivery.

cards.front: Where can key influencers be found?
cards.back: Senior executives; people doing day-to-day work in user, supplier and operational communities; people at information, knowledge and money bottlenecks; people who shape majority perception; those the team works closest with.

cards.front: The three project interests?
cards.back: Business, user and supplier. Each sits partly in the organizational ecosystem and partly in the project ecosystem.

cards.front: Define culture.
cards.back: The set of shared attitudes, values, goals and ways of working that characterize a group of people.

cards.front: Where is the shared understanding of the project captured?
cards.back: In the project brief. The resulting ways of working are captured in the management approaches.

cards.front: When should the shared understanding be checked?
cards.back: At the end of each stage and whenever there is a change in key influencers.

cards.front: What does persistent non-compliance with project processes often indicate?
cards.back: That the agreed ways of working no longer match the emerging project culture. Explore the disconnect rather than assuming poor behaviour.

cards.front: Collaboration versus co-creation?
cards.back: Collaboration is people across the ecosystem working together. Co-creation is collaboration that involves users and key influencers in designing products and ways of working so they are adopted.

cards.front: Leadership versus management?
cards.back: Leadership motivates people toward objectives through collaboration and influence. Management instructs the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working.

cards.front: Why do project teams need a different leadership style from business teams?
cards.back: They are temporary, cross boundaries, have multiple reporting lines and competing priorities, so a temporary leader finds it harder to exercise authority.

cards.front: What is cultural intelligence?
cards.back: The capability to relate and work across cultures within the organizational ecosystem.

cards.front: What should be clear about work outside the project scope that the project depends on?
cards.back: The dependencies, who is responsible, and how it is funded and monitored.

cards.front: What is psychological safety in a team?
cards.back: Members feel accepted, respected and able to express diverse views without fear of negative consequences. Everyone is responsible for creating it.

cards.front: Five ways PRINCE2 supports effective teams?
cards.back: Project plan; team structure and role descriptions; communication management approach; project initiation documentation; product-based planning.

cards.front: How is social cohesion built?
cards.back: Regular purposeful meetings, planning how key relationships develop over the project, and considering co-location. Virtual teams add co-location days, informal online time, away days and chances to meet.

cards.front: Purpose of the communication management approach?
cards.back: To define the means and frequency of communicating with and getting feedback from the project ecosystem, through a controlled two-way flow of information.

cards.front: Contents of the communication management approach?
cards.back: Scope; stakeholder analysis; communications schedule and procedures; responsibilities; resources; supporting tools and techniques; standards; references.

cards.front: Why is communication as much about listening as broadcasting?
cards.back: To understand perceptions and concerns so they are addressed before they become risks, and to tailor messages to each group.

cards.front: What is a quiet phase?
cards.back: Keeping wider communication minimal while a small group of key influencers develops the project, to limit rumour and misinformation. Useful for complex, wide-impact or politically sensitive projects.

cards.front: Why not rely only on periodic reporting?
cards.back: Reporting can be biased, as people subconsciously shape information. Add other routes: relationships with key influencers and monitoring the health of key relationships.

cards.front: What do pockets of resistance tell you?
cards.back: Where communication should be focused. Listen to find misconceptions and address issues.

cards.front: The three people-focused activities central to the method?
cards.back: Leading successful change, leading successful teams and communication.

cards.front: The five integrated elements of PRINCE2?
cards.back: Principles, people, practices, processes and the project context.

cards.front: How do stage boundaries relate to people?
cards.back: They often mark a change in influencers and key relationships, and are good points to review the skills needed next and change people, even on the project board.

cards.front: What does the extent of delegation under manage by exception depend on?
cards.back: The level of confidence and trust in the key relationships, which adapts as skills and capabilities develop.

cards.front: Which practice explains how people organize in the temporary team?
cards.back: Organizing.

cards.front: The four layers of the PRINCE2 processes?
cards.back: Business, directing, managing and delivering.
